title: ‘One Piece’ Season 3 Casts Its Koza, Toto, Pell and Chaka
description:
Netflix has added four to the cast of “One Piece” Season 3, casting the roles of Koza, Toto, Pell and Chaka. 

	Emilio Sakraya (“Rheingold”) will pl
body:
Netflix has added four to the cast of “One Piece” Season 3, casting the roles of Koza, Toto, Pell and Chaka. 

	Emilio Sakraya (“Rheingold”) will play Koza, Omid Abtahi (The Mandalorian”) will play Toto, Jamie Ward (“The Gentlemen”) will play Pell and Nabeel Khan (“Mandela: Long Walk to Freedom”) plays Chaka. 

	Returning for the third season, which is officially titled “One Piece: The Battle of Alabasta,” are Iñaki Godoy as Monkey D. Luffy, Mackenyu as Zoro, Emily Rudd as Nami, Jacob Romero as Usopp, Taz Skylar as Sanji, Charithra Chandran as Miss Wednesday, Mikaela Hoover as Chopper, Joe Manganiello as Mr. 0, Lera Abova as Miss All Sunday and Sendhil Ramamurthy as Nefartari Cobra. 
	

	Season 3 newcomers include Cole Escola as Bon Clay, Xolo Maridueña as Portgas D. Ace, Daisy Head as Miss Doublefinger and Awdo Awdo as Mr. 1. 


	Following the events of the show’s sophomore season, war is brewing for Monkey D. Luffy and the Straw Hat gang in Alabasta, Princess Vivi’s homeland. Per the series logline, “a rebellion threatens to tear the nation apart, fueled in secret by one of the Seven Warlords of the Sea, the ruthless Sir Crocodile, and his underground syndicate Baroque Works, who seek to conquer Alabasta for themselves. In a season defined by unbreakable bonds and impossible choices, the Straw Hats must face a brewing civil war and a powerful warlord to save Vivi’s kingdom before it crumbles into the sand.”

	Joe Tracz and Ian Stokes serve as co-showrunners, writers and executive producers. “One Piece” was created in partnership with Shueisha and produced by Tomorrow Studios and Netflix. 
	

	Executive producing are Eiichiro Oda, Marty Adelstein and Becky Clements through Tomorrow Studios, Tetsu Fujimura, Chris Symes, Christoph Schrewe and Steven Maeda. Production for Season 3 of the pirate adventure has wrapped in Cape Town, South Africa

title: Taylor Sheridan Accused of Stealing ‘Yellowstone’ From 2016 Pitch in Copyright Lawsuit
description: Writer Lauren J. Salkin has accused Taylor Sheridan of stealing his marquee series “Yellowstone” from her 2016 pitch in a lawsuit filed on Friday. 1
body:
Writer Lauren J. Salkin has accused Taylor Sheridan of stealing his marquee series “Yellowstone” from her 2016 pitch in a lawsuit filed on Friday. 101 Studios, Paramount and Elevate Entertainment are also listed as defendants.

	Reps for Sheridan, 101 Studios, Paramount and Elevate Entertainment did not immediately respond to Variety’s request for comment.

	In the court documents, obtained by Variety, Salkin alleges that she pitched her own sprawling Western drama, “Sovereign Nation,” to Sheridan’s management company, Elevate Entertainment, in 2016, only to be told: “Taylor thanks you very much for your interest. Unfortunately, he’s unavailable for TV projects.” The suit then claims that “Yellowstone” was greenlit at Paramount “within months” of her rejection.
	

	“Sheridan, however, was not ‘unavailable for TV projects,’” the suit reads, “Instead, he and others used Salkin’s copyrighted works to develop Yellowstone. On June 20, 2018, Paramount Network aired its first episode.”


	The lawsuit lists several “specific expressive choices” that “Yellowstone” allegedly lifted from Salkin’s “Sovereign Nation.” Those elements, the suit states, include “a tribal casino functioning as the institutional center of political and development power; a signature confrontation staged in the tribal chairman’s casino office over expansion beyond reservation boundaries; the use of trust land, the absence of zoning restrictions, and a 99-year lease structure as the concrete mechanism for that expansion; and recurring master-plan imagery deployed to dramatize the struggle for territorial control.”
	

	Salkin’s lawyers also claim that she “proposed” Danny Huston and Gil Birmingham for “Sovereign Nation” in her pitch deck. Both were later cast in “Yellowstone” and played “materially parallel structural roles: Birmingham as the tribal political leader whose authority and development strategy run through the casino, and Huston as the outside development power broker who supplies the political or commercial path for that expansion.”

	The suit later states, “When the works are objectively compared, the same coordinated design repeatedly appears: casino-centered institutions organize political power; the same unusual land-development mechanisms propel the conflict; parallel scenes perform the same dramatic functions; and the same actors appear in materially parallel roles. These are not merely convergences of a shared genre. Taken together with access and timing, they support a strong inference of copying.”

schema.headline: Taylor Sheridan Accused of Stealing ‘Yellowstone’ From 2016 Pitch in Copyright Lawsuit

title: ‘Skintown’ Review: A Breezy, Loved-Up, Drugged-Up Guide to Getting Into Trouble in The Troubles
description: Nostalgia, like ecstasy, is a hell of a drug and Kieron J. Walsh’s warm-hearted, hot-headed “Skintown” is buzzing on both. A more polite brother to
body:
Nostalgia, like ecstasy, is a hell of a drug and Kieron J. Walsh’s warm-hearted, hot-headed “Skintown” is buzzing on both. A more polite brother to the “Kneecap” boys and a more cautious cousin to those “Derry Girls” still, the Fermanagh-set friendship comedy sends fizzy, sweetly chemical energy coursing through a rave-romanticizing riff on the coming-of-age formula. The story may not be exactly new, but its bittersweet life lessons are delivered with such retroactive affection and such eagerness by the appealing cast, that if you’re of a mind to complain, well, in the parlance of the movie, would you ever give over, catch yourself on and wise up. 
	

	It is 1994, in Enniskillen, unflatteringly dubbed “Skintown” by its denizens and famous for “a lake, an old castle and an IRA bomb that killed 11 civilians in 1987.” Vinny (Jack Rowan) wants nothing more than to get the hell out. Partly, that’s due to the omnipresent dangers of an intractable conflict that has been ongoing since before he was born. (Vinny is 23, though his characterization here skews younger.) But really his disillusion with Skintown is an independence struggle of a more personal kind — one recognisable to anybody who remembers their jaundiced familiarity with their childhood hometown starting to curdle into contempt as adulthood beckoned. When Vinny strikes up an unlikely friendship with Wilson (Hope Ipoku Jr.) a Black squaddie from Manchester who’s been deployed to serve in the universally despised British military patrols, they bond when he realises that for Wilson, joining the army was his escape from the place he grew up in.
	

	Still, as soon as Vinny gets the money together, he’s resolved to leave, although there are things he’ll miss: his supportive, hardworking paramedic mum (Roisin Gallagher); his peppy unrequited crush Eileen (Jamie Lee O’Donnell); and most of all, his best mate Jonty (Chris Walley), a shell-suited, high-spirited raver just out to have a good time. Vinny and Jonty are as thick as the thieves they eventually, inadvertently become when they’re pressganged into a caper involving a load of ecstasy stolen from the UVF (a loyalist paramilitary group).

	On the bright side, though — and DP Ruairi O’Brien’s pleasant images make most everything bright even when, among sparse crowds and street scenes that feel rigidly dressed to the camera, the limits of the budget show — if they manage to sell the drugs and survive, they stand to make quite a bit of cash. More, anyway, than they could hope to score from their part-time jobs at the neighborhood pizzeria, whose oleaginous owner, splendidly named Tony Pepperoni (Michael Smiley), insists on serving his pizzas with a side of Peking ribs because, he contends, “the Irish aren’t ready for pizza on its own. They need a wee side of ribs to wean them off the Chinese.”

	That kind of authentically eccentric observation feels lifted directly from experience, and the pacy screenplay, adapted by Enniskillen native Ciarán McMenamin from his 2018 novel, abounds in such flourishes. As a ritual, the whole pub greets the TV newsreader (modelled on BBC institution Moira Stuart) like an old friend every time she begins her report with “Good evening.” “Body of Christ,” blasphemes Jonty benignly, handing out pills at a rave like they’re communion wafers. And, it being marching season, everyone is used to maneuvering around the Orangemen who take to parading down the main street at the drop of a bowler hat. “They’d want to get a move on if they’re planning on stopping outside every Catholic pub,” sighs barmaid Chalky (Tara Lynn O’Neill) resignedly. 

	Ah yes, the Catholics. The Protestants. The Republicans. The Unionists. The IRA, the UVF, the UDA, the INLA, the RUC, the Brits and the Battle of the Boyne — Vinny’s rather unnecessary voiceover namechecks them all, with more or less equal disparagement. While he and his mates are from a Catholic/Republican background, “Skintown” is careful not to overtly assign blame to one side and virtue to the other. Instead, most of its rancor is directed without sectarian bias, at the politician class. The brief, incredulous euphoria that follows the fateful announcement of an IRA ceasefire, is immediately dampened by one barfly (Belfast-born icon Lalor Roddy) observing drily, “If there’s any conceivable way to fuck this up, those politicians will find it.”
	

	This careful avoidance of any alienating perspective, and its streak of sentimentality make “Skintown” a more timid proposition than, say, “Kneecap,” even as it ramps up to an inevitable tragedy to undercut the bursts of MDMA-infused idealism elsewhere. But it also serves up a gently pointed reminder that for all the region was internationally synonymous with terrorism, reprisal and violent death, most of its inhabitants were ordinary people just going about the humdrum business of everyday life. And being Northern Irish, they did it with an indomitable sense of humor. So don’t come to “Skintown” for trenchant political commentary; come for the slangy jokes, the ’90s kitsch and the precise evocation of the love/hate relationship so many of us Irish have with the place that, however begrudgingly, we call home.

schema.headline: ‘Skintown’ Review: A Breezy, Loved-Up, Drugged-Up Guide to Getting Into Trouble in The Troubles

title: Venice-Bound ‘Meteorite,’ Debut Feature From Colombia’s Sebastián Múnera, Acquired by MoreThan Films (EXCLUSIVE)
description: MoreThan Films has acquired Colombian filmmaker Sebastián Múnera‘s film “Meteorite,” which will have its world premiere in Venice Critics’ Week (Sep
body:
MoreThan Films has acquired Colombian filmmaker Sebastián Múnera‘s film “Meteorite,” which will have its world premiere in Venice Critics’ Week (Sept. 2-12).

	The film follows Tefa and Nia, who live in a small town near the Magdalena River, where they raise Nia’s young nephew. Nia persuades Tefa to join her in smuggling cellphones into the regional prison. Their journey leads them through an extravagant amusement park built on the grounds of a drug lord’s former estate.
	

	“As they wander among water slides, verdant paths, and concrete dinosaurs, disquieting memories whisper in the summer heat. In a landscape where violence lingers beneath every surface, Tefa is drawn toward an inevitable encounter,” according to the synopsis.


	Queralt Pons Serra, managing partner at MoreThan Films, said, “What excited us about ‘Meteorite’ from the beginning was the strength and singularity of Sebastián’s gaze. You can really feel his artistic background in the way he approaches images, spaces and textures, creating a world that is incredibly cinematic, beautiful and also deeply emotional. There is something very immersive and atmospheric about the film that stayed with us long after watching it.”

	Múnera is a Colombian visual artist and filmmaker. He was a resident at the Cité Internationale des Arts in Paris, invited by the Centre Georges Pompidou. His films have been selected at festivals such as IFFR Rotterdam, DOK Leipzig and FICCI Cartagena. He has received distinctions including the Humberto Solás Cine en Construcción Award and the International Symposium on Auteur Cinema Altiplano Incuba Award.
	

	“Meteorite,” his first fiction feature, was awarded at work-in-progress programs in Málaga and Cartagena.

	The producers are Sebastian Martinez, Mauricio S. Burckhardt (Haus Kino), Valeria Mejia, Sebastián Múnera (Entre Acto), Abel Villa Romero, Deimer Quintero Vertel (Archipiélago Sonoro) and Rodrigo Ramos (Pos[T] La Casa).

schema.headline: Venice-Bound ‘Meteorite,’ Debut Feature From Colombia’s Sebastián Múnera, Acquired by MoreThan Films (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Upendra Joins Cast as Teja Sajja, Shanaya Kapoor, Suparn S. Varma’s Sequel Titled ‘Zombie Reddy Nxt Lvl’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Kannada cinema superstar Upendra has joined the cast of “Zombie Reddy Nxt Lvl,” the sequel to the hit “Zombie Reddy,” in a powerhouse role, India’s
body:
Kannada cinema superstar Upendra has joined the cast of “Zombie Reddy Nxt Lvl,” the sequel to the hit “Zombie Reddy,” in a powerhouse role, India’s People Media Factory has confirmed. 

	The announcement, made on star Teja Sajja‘s birthday, also confirms the film’s cast and creative team.

	The adventure zombie action-comedy marks the South Indian cinema debut of “Tu Yaa Main” star Shanaya Kapoor. Teja Sajja returns as the franchise’s zombie-slaying lead.
	

	Directed by Prasanth Varma, “Zombie Reddy” was released in 2021, and followed a game developer who must save his village after a scientist’s vaccine experiment unleashes a zombie outbreak. 


	Suparn S. Varma, known for Prime Video’s “The Family Man” Season 2, Netflix’s “Rana Naidu” and film “Haq,” directs the sequel from a story created by Prasanth Varma. Gowra Hari, whose scores powered “HanuMan” and “Mirai,” composes the music.

	Hussain Dalal, Prasanth Varma and Suparn S. Varma wrote the screenplay. T.G. Vishwa Prasad and Krithi Prasad produce for People Media Factory. The film will release in seven languages – Hindi, Telugu, Kannada, Tamil, Malayalam, Nepali and Japanese.

	“The biggest takeaway from my career is that cinema survives on audacity, not formulas,” Teja Sajja said. “When ‘Zombie Reddy’ was made, it was a calculated risk born out of a desire to break the monotony of conventional storytelling. I can’t thank the audience enough for embracing me as a zombie slayer and their unbridled curiosity and faith in what I do next. It’s the love that I’ve received over the years that pushes me to make brave choices. So here’s a promise to take the mayhem to a whole new scale in ‘Zombie Reddy Nxt Lvl.’ As I turn a year older, the zombies turn deadlier. With the audience validating everyone associated with the film, I’m all set to fight the dead onscreen like never before. It makes me very proud to be part of a team that wants to give viewers a grand, immersive spectacle that feeds their appetite for the extraordinary.”
	

	Suparn S. Varma said the goal was to surprise both himself and the audience with something unlike anything seen before. “Zombies have always been a fascinating expression of our worst catastrophes, and with this film, we wanted to take that idea to the next level,” he said. “We’ve taken the foundational brilliance that Prasanth Varma created and blown it wide open, building a never-seen-before zombieverse. It’s been an absolute treat to explore a genre with such enormous creative possibilities and collaborate with stalwarts who bring their own seasoned finesse to the film. Here’s wishing one of them – the audience’s superstar and favourite zombie slayer, Teja Sajja, a very happy birthday!”

	T.G. Vishwa Prasad said People Media Factory has always aimed to push the boundaries of commercial cinema. “‘Zombie Reddy Nxt Lvl’ is an epic adventure designed for a global audience, which is why we are releasing it from India to Japan,” he said. “Everything is next level right from the actors starring in it to the director, technicians, and music. The scale is massive, the stakes are dead or alive, and we cannot wait to bring this zombieverse to audiences in 2027.”

	Despite HBO Max hiking prices again last fall, the streamer is hoping to win over some new customers, with a 7-day free trial through Prime Video, just in time for the buzzy premiere of “Lanterns” and awards season pushes for critically-acclaimed shows like “Hacks” and “The Pitt.”

	While Amazon usually saves its streaming deals for Prime Day, this HBO Max offer is live on the site now and open to all Prime members with no promo code or contract required. In order to access the free trial, you’ll have to sign up for an Amazon Prime account (which also offers a 30-day free trial) and navigate to the Prime Channels hub. From there, find the HBO Max landing page and select the free trial offer.


	If you already have a Prime account, you can just sign in and add an HBO Max account free of charge. Once the week-long trial ends, the ad-supported HBO Max subscription will resume at its regular price of $10.99/month.

	There’s never been a better time to add an HBO Max subscription (formerly “Max”) to your Prime Video streaming arsenal. HBO Max has had an exciting lineup of can’t-miss new releases for 2026, including “DTF St. Louis,” the return of Lisa Kudrow’s “The Comeback” and the “Big Bang Theory” spin-off, “Stuart Fails to Save the Universe.”

	Returning favorites this year also included the third season of “The White Lotus” and the final season of “Euphoria.”

	HBO Max also has hundreds of new films on its roster, including “Marty Supreme,” “The Drama,” “Wuthering Heights,” “We Live in Time,” “Dune: Part Two” and “Joker Folie à Deux,” in addition to beloved shows such as “The Sopranos,” “The Wire” and “Curb Your Enthusiasm.”


	HBO Max doesn’t offer a free trial on its own site, so the Prime Video deal is one of the only ways to get the streaming service for free. Worth noting: Amazon has removed this offer from its Prime streaming hub in the past without warning, so we recommend taking advantage of the free trial while it’s still live.

	You can also get HBO Max for free through DirecTV, which offers a free subscription when you sign-up for the streamer’s MyEntertainment Genre Pack. Plans start at $42.99/month and get you 60+ live TV channels plus HBO Max, Disney+ and Hulu for free. See the DirecTV deal here.

title: ‘One Battle After Another’ and ‘Marty Supreme’ Take Top Honors at Location Managers Guild International Awards
description:
“One Battle After Another” and “Marty Supreme” took top honors at the Location Managers Guild International (LMGI) LMGI Awarda.

	The LGMI Awards we
body:
“One Battle After Another” and “Marty Supreme” took top honors at the Location Managers Guild International (LMGI) LMGI Awarda.

	The LGMI Awards were handed out on Saturday night and honor the use of filming locations across motion pictures, television, commercials, film commissions, and special achievement categories. 

	Paul Thomas Anderson’s “One Battle After Another” won outstanding locations in a contemporary feature film. It was shot across California’s Humboldt County, Sacramento, Stockton, Eureka, Arcata, San Diego and El Paso, Texas. Josh Safdie’s “Marty Supreme” won outstanding locations in a period feature film for its work across New York City, greater New York, the Hudson Valley, New Jersey and Tokyo.
	

	“Pluribus,” “Fallout” and “Black Rabbit” were the television winners. “Pluribus” was filmed in Albuquerque, New Mexico, Montana, Nevada, and Spain, and won outstanding locations in a contemporary television series. “Fallout,” shot in California’s Dumont Dunes, Mojave Desert, Antelope Valley and Santa Clarita,” won outstanding locations in a period television series. Filmed around New York City, including Brooklyn and Manhattan, “Black Rabbit” won outstanding locations in a tv anthology, movie or limited series. 


	Four-time Emmy-winning director and writer Vince Gilliga received the Eva Monley Award for his dedication to storytelling through location over his career and his most recent work on “Pluribus.”

	Mike Fantasia, location manager of films including “Top Gun: Maverick,” “Killers of the Flower Moon” and “Spider-Man: Homecoming” was presented the Lifetime Achievement Award. 
	

	“Celebrating our LMGI winners was a truly remarkable experience,” Nancy Haecker, LMGI Awards Chair, said. “The ceremony was a powerful celebration of achievement, filled with inspiring moments and well-deserved recognition, beautifully capped by the genius of Vince Gilligan. Each of this year’s winners is incredibly deserving, and it was a distinct privilege to honor their talent, dedication, and outstanding contributions to our industry.”

	Winners list below.

	OUTSTANDING LOCATIONS IN A CONTEMPORARY FEATURE FILM

	“One Battle After Another” (Warner Bros. Pictures)

	Michael Glaser / LMGI, Michael Wesley / LMGI, Rich Heichel / LMGI

	OUTSTANDING LOCATIONS IN A PERIOD FEATURE FILM

	“Marty Supreme” (A24)

	Matthew Kania, Ross Brodar / LMGI

	OUTSTANDING LOCATIONS IN A CONTEMPORARY TELEVISION SERIES

	“Pluribus” (Apple TV+)

	Christian Diaz de Bedoya / LMGI, John O’Connor, Priscila Calero, Jorge Noguerales,

	Yanira De Armas, Will Brewster

	OUTSTANDING LOCATIONS IN A PERIOD TELEVISION SERIES

	“Fallout” – Season 2 (Amazon Prime Video)

	Mandi Dillin / LMGI, David Park / LMGI

	OUTSTANDING LOCATIONS IN A TV ANTHOLOGY, MOVIE OR LIMITED SERIES

	“Black Rabbit” (Netflix)

	Paul Eskenazi, Joel McGlumphy

	OUTSTANDING FILM COMMISSION/ OFFICE

	Humboldt-Del Norte Film Commission: “One Battle After Another” (Warner Bros. Pictures)

	Cassandra Hesseltine

	OUTSTANDING LOCATIONS IN A COMMERCIAL

	TOYOTA TRUCKS: “They Don’t Read Reviews”

title: ‘Sentimental Value’ Sweeps Amanda Awards
description: Joachim Trier’s Oscar winner “Sentimental Value” became this year’s biggest Amanda Awards winner, taking home eight statuettes, including the top pr
body:
Joachim Trier’s Oscar winner “Sentimental Value” became this year’s biggest Amanda Awards winner, taking home eight statuettes, including the top prize for best Norwegian film. 

	Trier was also awarded for directing, as well as his screenplay written with longtime collaborator Eskil Vogt.

	“There’s a lot of stuff going on when you make and release films, and we both like to go back to that safe space and rediscover that calm where it’s just our two voices. We are fortunate enough that our films generate more and more noise that we have to shut out, so when we work, we make it personal and small again,” they told Variety back in January.
	

	“When I write alone, I procrastinate. When I’m procrastinating with Joachim, even if I haven’t done anything, at least I got to spend a day with my friend,” said Vogt, with Trier adding: “Eskil is my longest relationship outside of my parents. We don’t need to be silly romantic about it, but we have to be honest: it’s a real gift.”


	Paul Thomas Anderson’s hit “One Battle After Another” tok home the Amanda For best foreign film.

	On the acting front, Pia Tjelta scored her second Amanda – this time for her performance in “Don’t Call Me Mama.” Inga Ibsdotter Lilleaas won for “Sentimental Value,” while Anna Drakopoulou Sverrisdóttir was named Newcomer of the Year for “Brightly Shining.”

	“The Battle of Oslo” – last year’s opening film at the Norwegian International Film Festival Haugesund – won the People’s Amanda.

	It depicts the sinking of German cruiser Blücher, under the leadership of Colonel Birger Eriksen, and “is one of the most famous events in our history. Some people are calling it the single most important event during the WWII in Norway,” said director Daniel Fahre.
	

	“We kept it quite accurate, also because it’s such a thrilling story. But we had to look for its emotional side, because there’s no mention of that in military reports. I am sure Colonel Eriksen had doubts, that he was afraid. But nobody wrote about it. I wanted to follow the facts and see what was hiding behind them.” 

	The Amanda Committee’s Honorary Award went to Per Christian Ellefsen, known for “Elling” and called by the jurors “one of Norway’s most beloved actors.” 

	“The first film about Elling was released in 2001, meaning it celebrates its 25th anniversary this year, and Per Christian Ellefsen was nominated for an Amanda Award for the title role in the first film,” they recalled, saying that “few characters in Norwegian cinema have been as beloved.” 

	“While he struggles through three successful films, Per Christian Ellefsen certainly masters the role of Elling to perfection,” they said.

	Finally, the Amanda Committee’s Golden Clapper went to casting directirs Mette Holme Nielsen and Jannecke Bervell for their contributions to Norwegian film over more than 30 years. 

	“Casting is one of the most crucial elements in film and TV production, yet it is also one of the most underrated. It is in the casting process that the script meets the actors, and this is where the foundation for credibility, chemistry, and cohesion is laid,” argued the jury.

	“A good casting can elevate an entire production, while poor casting can bring a film down. Casting also plays an important role in promoting diversity, by opening the doors to new voices, new expressions and a broader range of people on screen. It is therefore a profession that requires instinct, an understanding of people, experience and the ability to see potential where others may not.”

	Mette Holme Nielsen is known for “Kitchen Stories” and “Utøya July 22,” which earned her a nomination for the International Casting Director Award. Jannecke Bervell worked on “Elling,” “Kon-Tiki” or “The Quake.” 

	The Amanda Awards were hosted by Vegard Larsen and Linnea Myhre. The broadcast was produced by Monster for NRK. 

	The full list of awards:

	Best Norwegian Film 

	“Sentimental Value” 
	

	Director: Joachim Trier

	Producers: Maria Ekerhovd and Andrea Berentsen Ottmar

	Best Director

	Joachim Trier for “Sentimental Value”

	Best Screenplay

	Eskil Vogt and Joachim Trier for “Sentimental Value”

	Best Performance in a Leading Role

	Pia Tjelta for “Don’t Call Me Mama”

	Best Performance in a Supporting Role

	Inga Ibsdotter Lilleaas for “Sentimental Value”

	Newcomer of the Year

	Anna Drakopoulou Sverrisdóttir for “Brightly Shining”

	Best Childrens’ Film

	“A Mouse Hunt for Christmas” 

	Director: Henrik Martin Dahlsbakken

	Producers: Martin Sundland, Thea B. Kevin Karlsen and Tor Markus Iden

	Best Documentary 

	“Flophouse America” Director: Monica Strømdahl

	Producers: Siri Natvik and Beathe Hofseth

	Best Production Design

	Jørgen Stangebye Larsen for “Sentimental Value”

	The People’s Amanda

	“The Battle of Oslo”

	Director: Daniel Fahre

	Producer: Knut Inge Solbu

	Best Sound Design 

	Johannes Dekko for “Rally from Paris to the Pyramids”

	Best Makeup Design

	Trine Morland for “Sentimental Value”

	Best Editing

	Olivier Bugge Coutté for “Sentimental Value”

title: Dale Morris, Titan of Nashville Management Who Forged Superstar Careers for Kenny Chesney and Alabama, Dies at 89
description: Dale Morris, one of the leading names in the ranks of Nashville music managers, who helped build up superstar careers for the group Alabama and then
body:
Dale Morris, one of the leading names in the ranks of Nashville music managers, who helped build up superstar careers for the group Alabama and then Kenny Chesney nearly from scratch, died Friday at 89. A representative said Morris died in his sleep.

	“He lived a big, bold, beautiful, blessed life, and I’m holding onto that right now,” said his protege and eventually managerial partner of many years, Clint Higham, president of Morris Higham Management.  “It’s the end of an era.”
	

	Morris met the fledgling Alabama in 1979 while heading up Dale Morris & Associates and played a massive role in making the group the most successful band in the history of country music, with 33 No. 1 hits in the 1980s and ’90s, along with a huge touring career that led to their being named Entertainer of the Year three times by the Country Music Association and five times by the Academy of Country Music in the mid-’80s. Alabama’s meteoric rise saw the group being credited for being early in country music to adopt some of rock’s touring production values, finding rock-star-level success as well.


	Lightning struck twice for Morris, as he oversaw the rise of Chesney from a country also-ran into the genre’s most reliable stadium-filler, who was named Entertainer of the Year four times in the 2000s by both the CMAs and ACMs, and who has enjoyed 32 No. 1 Billboard country smashes.

	Other artists Morris steered included Old Dominion, Ricky Van Shelton, Jerry Lee Lewis and his very first management client going back into the late ’60s, Bobby “Crash” Craddock.

	Said Higham, “He was larger than life, and never met a dream he couldn’t build. Dale Morris gave me my first internship, and I never wanted to go anywhere else. He saw things in people, in me, in Kenny, and inspired everyone to reach beyond what we thought possible. Maybe it’s how much he loved life, loved his family, loved us.”
	

	Chesney devoted significant passages in his 2025 book, “Heart Life Music,” to describing his relationship with Morris, which came about from him being a huge fan of Alabama and discovering there was a man behind the scenes making it happen.

	“By the time I came into Dale Morris’s orbit, he’d been to the top of the mountain with Alabama and redefined what was possible in country music,” Chesney wrote in his book, co-authored with Holly Gleason. “Alabama not only won all the awards, sold millions of albums, had iconic hit after iconic hit, they’d created a new mainstream country star who actually looked like their audience… Alabama was high energy, the drums were rock and roll; Jeff Cook played fancy guitars and Randy Owen’s voice had this believability.” Watching the band roll into town for a concert, as a fan, Chesney noticed “there had been a fifth person. A man with white hair, I figured might have been someone’s father. Over time, I realized their manager had been the one to see around corners, didn’t do business the way everyone else did, made a space for a band who’d shown up looking like their fans. He didn’t care about anything but getting the music to the fans—and that was me, standing in a field, waiting for Alabama to arrive.”



	

					Dale Morris
									Morris Higham Management
	



	When Chesney finally got the chance to meet with Morris as an aspiring artist, he said, the manager “also asked hard questions, really digging in on what it took… ‘How hard are you willing to work?’ ‘How far will you go when it’s so hard and it’s not happening?’ I would have said anything to get Dale Morris to manage me…

	“We talked about country music. Even more than Alabama, how songs and charisma were such a part of it, that spoke to country people,” Chesney continued. “He told me his story. The similarities emerged. He was from South Carolina, another small Southern town with heart and people who all knew one another. He worked hard, to build a life, to create something more. He’d been a salesman, and he had that used car salesman thing where he could slap you on the back, be a good ole boy like your best friend.

	“He loved music, made friends, some people thought he could be a manager. He started with Billy “Crash” Craddock, doing booking, picking up Jerry Lee Lewis. Successful, but he wanted something more. He’d seen a band in Myrtle Beach, who’d put out an independent record. They needed help. Dale applied himself. Once he and Alabama got going, they were in it together. When he realized arenas weren’t paying country acts like the rock bands, he took his band to the fields. Literally, set up a stage, charged a fair price for the fans, and tripled their money. … 
	

	“Classy, grateful, and humble, he knew how to make deals and close. I had a friend who called him ‘Make a Deal Dale’,” Chesney wrote. “He was raw, too. No airs, just unfiltered honesty about how rough it could be. He had relationships with everybody: labels, radio stations, big promoters, TV people, and publishers, but also the fair buyers, the country bar owners, the folks out in America who held careers together. We were gonna need them even more.

	“I didn’t bother meeting with another manager. Dale loved the game, and he loved coming up with new ways to do it. If I was willing to work as hard as I said, maybe I was the kid who’d  let him do it all over again. He didn’t believe in contracts. Didn’t have one with Alabama, didn’t need one with me. He said, ‘Let’s do it.'”

	Before taking on management, Morris began his career as a songwriter, reaching the top 5 in 1967 with a cut by Johnny Paycheck, “Don’t Monkey With Another Monkey’s Monkey.” He was inspired by that hit to move more into the business side, at first doing radio promo work for Little Darlin’ Records, before he joined producer Ron Chancey in starting Cartwheel Records. Their success with Billy “Crash” Craddock led resulted in ABC purchasing the label, which spurred Morris to move on to exploring management, starting International House of Talent, where he both managed and booked Craddock. 

	It was a decade into his management career that he discovered Alabama, with an agency arm, Dale Morris & Associates, booking shows for the group and finding increasingly large venues that few country acts of the time were playing. As Alabama’s shows grew, Morris realized other needs created by the group’s growth and purchased Bob Seger’s sound system in order to found Morris Leasing, which later became Morris Lighting + Sound.

	In 2010, Morris was elected into the International Talent Buyers Association Hall of Fame.

	He received the T.J. Martell Foundation’s Tony Martell Lifetime Entertainment Achievement Award in 2014 (at which he is pictured holding his trophy alongside Chesney, at top).

	Higham rose to become Morris’ partner after starting as an intern. In 2018, the two of them sold their booking agency part of their company to Paradigm Talent Agency (now The-Team), while continuing to hold onto the management division.
	

	In an interview with Pollstar that year, Morris said, “We’ve elected to stay small rather than to try to sign every act in the world. That way we were able to do what we were able to do and book and manage. Everybody seemed to be happy. We never signed contracts with any of the acts we represented. You come with us and if you want to leave us tomorrow, pay us what you owe us and out the door you go. That’s been our policy for at least 45 years.”

	Morris was married to his wife, Earline, for 68 years. He was preceded in death by a son, Tim. Survivors include the couple’s daughter-in-law, Jennifer, grandchildren Zack, Colton (and wife Mary Blair), Nick (and wife Shelby) and Kendall, and great grandchildren Mary Dee and Gus.

	“We’re so blessed to have had 90 years with him as the patriarch of our family,” said Zack Morris. “Thank you to our music industry family and to his vast community of friends in Nashville, Boca and beyond for loving him all these many years.”

	A celebration of life is being planned for this fall, with details to be announced in the weeks ahead.

schema.headline: Dale Morris, Titan of Nashville Management Who Forged Superstar Careers for Kenny Chesney and Alabama, Dies at 89

title: Karoline Leavitt's Post-White House Job Revealed
description:
Karoline Leavitt
                          New Trump-Focused Job Revealed
body:
Karoline Leavitt
                          New Trump-Focused Job Revealed
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 22, 2026
                            5:45 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 23, 2026
                                4:22 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Karoline Leavitt may be leaving the White House, but she’s not leaving Team Trump behind.
      
    
            The outgoing press secretary revealed she will still be supporting President Trump after she exits her role by working for MAGA Inc. -- the super PAC she previously worked for before becoming one of his right-hand people, NBC News reports.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            As we reported, Trump announced Leavitt's departure as press secretary earlier this month ... and she later noted she wanted to be home more to spend time with her two young children. She returned from maternity leave after welcoming her second child with real-estate developer Nicholas Riccio in May.
      

            She told reporters Friday she will miss the job ... but she loves her offspring more.
      
    
            Leavitt made the remarks as she departed Myrtle Beach, South Carolina Friday ... where she was with Trump and Natalie Harp for a campaign rally for U.S. Senator Darline Graham ... where Trump supported Graham -- despite being briefly heckled by a man with a violent message on his shirt.
      
    
            As you know, Natalie has been the center of attention lately as her relationship with Trump is scrutinized. Earlier this week, her brother, Preston, accused her of having "an unhealthy obsession" with the prez.
      
    
            But, Trump has continued to keep both Natalie and Karoline close ... and seems to be huge fans of them both.

            Enes Kanter Freedom wants to play in the WNBA next season ... but for this weekend, he'll be a spectator, 'cause the former NBA big man intends to attend the Fever vs. Sky game in Chicago, TMZ Sports has learned.
      
    
            The 6-foot-10 center is planning to make the trip to Wintrust Arena in Chi-Town for Sunday’s nationally televised matchup ... starring Caitlin Clark and Sophie Cunningham.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Our sources tell us Kanter is taking "major security measures" to ensure his safety at the arena.
      

            Kanter kicked a hornet's nest recently when he declared himself eligible for the '27 WNBA Draft, arguing the league's current self-identification guidelines mean he meets the requirements to compete.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            In fact, he even floated the idea of teaming up with Clark, joking the potential pairing would be a "modern Kobe and Shaq."
      
    
            The 11-year NBA vet has consistently framed his draft declaration as being about support for women, adamantly saying he's not mocking the trans community ... something his critics have accused him of doing.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Instagram Media.
      
    
            It's unclear if the WNBA, Fever and/or the Sky are aware of Kanter's plans, or whether they'll try and stop him from pulling up to the game on Sunday.
      
    
            The Fever vs. Sky tip-off tomorrow at 7 PM ET.

            Jay Leno wants courts in New Hampshire to recognize his wife's conservatorship in California so he can sell one of their New England properties ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            Jay says he's planning to sell some real estate he and his wife, Mavis, own in the Granite State ... hence the reason for the filing.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            TMZ obtained court docs filed earlier this month, where the comedian tells the court he wants to sell "certain real estate located in New Hampshire" that they hold as community property.
      

                    
                          
                                  
      
        
    
            The property in question appears to be a 2-bed, 2-bath ranch built in 1995 ... that he's listed for just under $400K. Jay put it up for sale back in June.
      
    
            He's been Mavis' caretaker throughout her battle with dementia.
      
    
            The court has yet to rule.
